questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The country and a university with courses relevant for my study

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy, the host university provided sufficient information

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Introduction meeting. Nothing else.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The orientation was fine, but it was mostly learning by finding out

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The university had limited rooms available that you could sign up for approximately 3-4 months before the beginning of the semester. It is crucial to look at their website for the dates of exchange student accommodation. The most important dates are actually the registration dates and not the actual dates of when the rooms are released, as the registration serves as a first come first served. Only university approved registrations will be able to get a room, and they only approve as many students as there are rooms, so the first students to register will be the ones that are approved.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: No meal plans. The cooking facilities were shared kitchens for 2 or 3 people, very decent but you have to buy your own utilities (pots, pans etc.)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are different locations: Hatta (which is literally on campus, and maybe a bit boring since you will spend most of your time at uni or at home), Blaauwe Molen (I lived here, and it is right inbetween uni and center of Rotterdam, which is a nice location in the best area of the city, a student bar just by the build and if you are lucky you can get a room with a balcony with views over the city and the river) and other places. I found that the prices were fairly decent, especially compared to the Social Hub (can also be booked through uni) which is more expensive.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you pay attention to registration dates it is not that difficult to get a room.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not much of a hassle, although you should be aware that Erasmus Rotterdam has a different understanding of the collaboration between KU and themselves. You have to make sure that Erasmus Rotterdam agrees with KU on the collaboration at a faculty level, I had to have KU to tell Erasmus Rotterdam that they collaborated with Erasmus School of Social and Behavioral Sciences down to the specific course-line (International Public Management and Public Policy)

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Other than the formal through the exchange system I just had to send some proof of language skills

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There is an exchange student hotline for each faculty which worked fine.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I registered for a premade course line (half of a one year master) and that was fairly easy.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Beware that you have courses of 5 ECTS so 6 courses in total and that they have 2 exam periods (one in fall and one in beginning of winter), and that it is very stressful if you choose to have 4 courses in the first part and two in the second part or vice versa. I would recommend 3 and 3 as it is best balanced.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Although the level of detail in the courses is less than at KU (probably because courses are only 5 ECTS compared to 7.5), they are very well put together the courses and you can expect a lot of reading and preparing for classes.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of courses is neither lesser or higher than at KU, however the way of teaching resembles High School more than university (at least as a Statskunskabs/Political Science student). There are many assignments during the actual course, there are presentations and the exams are often closed book meaning they focus more on your ability to remember and recite rather than your analytical and especially critical thinking. This means that the level is probably the same however there is a different focus requiring some adjustment.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Again the everyday classes resemble the Danish a lot, but maybe even more participatory than at KU. Expect that teachers will engage students alot, so come prepared for class and also expect a lot of closed book exams and less long written assignments.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
I was part of the International Public Management and Public Policy masters programme and had the following courses:
Global Governance
European Union Policy Making
Comparative Public Policy
International Organisations and Development
Europe in the World
International Public Management

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend taking the courses within one master, because all the different courses are related to each other especially the second part where the three courses draw on the previous three. This makes for a really nice cohesive experience

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I have no clue how my spending was divided but excluding rent which I paid sort of 1 to 1 with my Erasmus Grant I probably spent between 8000-10.000 kroner per month.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The groceries are around 25% cheaper than in Denmark. The beer is the same (tap beer) but they don't have cheap bottle beers, however their student bar is insanely cheap. Public transport is also expensive, so get an OV-chip card with a Flex subscription it will take 40% off prices outside rush hour with trains.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are so many sport facilities and clubs, it is very impressive!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They have all kinds of sport clubs and they have this exchange student social network but it is mostly (imo) for bachelor student, when you reach the age of 26 (like me) then 18 year old germans are not the most interesting company.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the nearby cities (Amsterdam, Delft, Den Haag, Gouda). Take the train to Beligum even! Other than that just discover all that Rotterdam has to offer, the museum card can be acquired for 20 euro giving you 1 euro access to all museums.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I mean you can go to so many countries and cities from Rottedam by train which is such a nice way to travel.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, Dutch people resemble Danes a lot.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk with the people in your class, it is very nice to have a social life with the people you study with, often many of the Dutch people also come from other cities so they are also looking for local friends.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Dutch people are pretty easy going

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Prepare accommodation well in advance, the housing crisis in the Netherlands is not a joke. If you want to learn dutch you have to apply already in beginning of August, however a lot of the courses are free. Also you need a bike so if you don't plan on bringing your own you have to be very quick at Swapfiets because they sell out.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't buy that ESN card, it is not very useful.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Actually it was my classmates.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Definitely the study, it was more challenging than I anticipated and I knew it was not going to be easy like in Southern or Eastern Europe

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Try the Kapsalon!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
